bill_summary: This bill consolidates and updates collective bargaining laws for State, public school, and community college employees. It establishes the Public Employee Relations Board (PERB) as an independent unit of State government to oversee these activities, replacing the State Labor Relations Board, the State Higher Education Labor Relations Board, and the Public School Labor Relations Board. The act standardizes procedures for establishing bargaining units, conducting elections for exclusive representatives, and resolving unfair labor practice disputes.
stakeholders: State employees, public school employees, community college faculty and staff, public employers (State agencies, local boards of education, and community colleges), and labor organizations (exclusive representatives).
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by at least 642,600 in FY 2024 to cover the personnel and operating costs of the new Public Employee Relations Board, including salaries for a full-time chair and three new deputy directors. Future annual expenditures are projected to increase to approximately 888,400 by FY 2028. Local expenditures are not expected to be materially affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Governor is responsible for appointing the five members of the newly established Public Employee Relations Board (PERB), including the chair, with the advice and consent of the Senate.

As a principal employer of state personnel, the Comptroller's office is subject to the collective bargaining laws modified by this act, and the Comptroller serves on the Board of Public Works which oversees related fiscal matters.
The Treasurer's Office oversees state funds and the retirement systems for public employees whose collective bargaining rights and procedures are restructured by this act.
The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies and boards; the fiscal note indicates that additional Assistant Attorneys General will be required to support the new Public Employee Relations Board.
DBM is the central personnel agency for the state and is directly responsible for collective bargaining for executive branch employees, whose governing laws are consolidated and altered by this bill.
The bill significantly restructures labor relations for public school systems by repealing the Public School Labor Relations Board and moving oversight to the new PERB.
The act explicitly includes independent home care providers (Medicaid) and other health-related personnel under the new consolidated collective bargaining framework.
MDOT is a primary public employer affected by the bill, with specific provisions relating to the bargaining units of the Maryland Transportation Authority police.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As a major employer of state personnel with extensive collective bargaining agreements, this agency is directly impacted by the consolidation and procedural changes in the Act.
State Police personnel are part of the executive branch workforce subject to the collective bargaining laws and procedural updates overseen by the new PERB.
This office assists the Governor in vetting and recommending candidates for the newly created Public Employee Relations Board.
The bill explicitly identifies the Maryland Environmental Service as a public employer subject to the revised collective bargaining statutes.
The bill establishes a specific and separate bargaining unit for the faculty at the Maryland School for the Deaf.
The act mandates a separate bargaining unit for Maryland Transportation Authority police officers at the rank of first sergeant and below.
Morgan State University is explicitly named as a public employer required to have separate bargaining units under the new consolidated labor relations framework.
The OAH is designated as a venue for hearings regarding unfair labor practice complaints issued by the Public Employee Relations Board.
The bill creates this board as the primary independent unit of state government responsible for overseeing collective bargaining for state, education, and higher education employees.
This board is abolished and its duties are consolidated into the newly established Public Employee Relations Board.
St. Mary's College is specifically named as a public employer that must maintain separate bargaining units under the Act.

agency_relevance.agency_name: State Higher Education Labor Relations Board
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This board is abolished and its functions are merged into the Public Employee Relations Board as part of the consolidation of labor laws.
As the state's largest higher education employer, USM institutions are explicitly required to maintain separate bargaining units under the new framework.
The agency manages benefits for state employees whose employment terms, wages, and working conditions are subject to the collective bargaining laws altered by this Act.
Employees of the Maryland Insurance Administration are specifically covered by the collective bargaining rights in Title 3 of the State Personnel and Pensions Article which this bill modifies.

Synopsis: Authorizing certain students who are at least 18 years old and under the age of 21 years to taste certain alcoholic beverages while participating in a course or program in enology, fermenting, brewing, or hospitality and tourism offered by a qualified institution of higher education without criminal penalty to the student, instructor, or institution of higher education under certain circumstances.
Title: Alcoholic Beverages – Use of Alcoholic Beverages for Educational Purposes

bill_summary: This bill allows students between 18 and 21 years old enrolled in specific higher education programs—such as enology, fermenting, brewing, or hospitality and tourism—to taste alcoholic beverages for educational purposes during class. The students are required to spit out the beverage after tasting and must be supervised by an authorized instructor. The bill exempts the students, instructors, and institutions from criminal penalties related to the possession or consumption of alcohol by individuals under the legal drinking age in these specific educational contexts.
responsible_party: Maryland Alcohol and Tobacco Commission and qualified institutions of higher education
stakeholders: Students aged 18 to 20 enrolled in brewing, enology, or hospitality programs; instructors at higher education institutions; and Maryland institutions of higher education.
fiscal_impact_summary: The Fiscal and Policy Note states that the bill is not anticipated to affect State or local government operations or finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill amends criminal statutes regarding the underage possession and consumption of alcohol, which affects the adjudication of such cases within the Maryland Judicial Branch.

As the state's principal tax collector and regulator of the alcohol industry, the Comptroller is impacted by the bill's provisions that exempt certain institutions of higher education from needing permits for educational alcohol tasting.
The bill relates to educational programs in hospitality, tourism, and brewing, which are key areas of workforce development and professional training overseen by the Department of Labor.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This agency advises the Governor on criminal justice strategies and public safety policy; the bill modifies criminal law regarding underage alcohol possession and consumption.

The Commission serves as the central regulatory board for Maryland's higher education institutions, which are the primary entities responsible for implementing and managing the educational programs and tasting activities authorized by the bill.

As the primary coordinating and regulatory board for postsecondary education, this agency ensures institutions meet the standards required to qualify for the educational exceptions provided in the bill.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The agency provides legal representation for indigent defendants in criminal cases; the bill creates a new legal exception and defense for underage alcohol possession in an educational context.
The State Police enforce state criminal and motor vehicle laws, including those related to underage drinking; the bill establishes a specific exception to these laws for educational purposes.

As an independent public university, Morgan State may offer courses in enology, brewing, or hospitality that would allow its students and instructors to utilize the legal protections provided by this bill.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the Governor, the General Assembly, and all state agencies, including the public colleges and the Higher Education Commission, regarding the implementation and legal interpretation of the bill.
As a public liberal arts college and independent state agency, the college may be directly impacted if it offers or plans to offer the qualifying educational programs mentioned in the bill.
The system oversees 12 public institutions, many of which offer programs in hospitality and fermentation science that will directly implement the policies authorized by this bill.

bill_summary: This bill modifies the Family and Medical Leave Insurance (FAMLI) Program by delaying the start date for employer and employee contributions to October 1, 2024, and the start date for benefit payments to January 1, 2026. It sets the cost-sharing split for contributions at 50% for employers and 50% for employees, caps the total contribution rate at 1.2% of wages, and mandates that the Maryland Department of Health reimburse certain community-based service providers for their share of contributions. Additionally, it eliminates the requirement that individuals exhaust all other employer-provided leave before receiving FAMLI benefits.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Labor and Maryland Department of Health
stakeholders: Maryland employees, employers with 15 or more employees, self-employed individuals participating in the program, and community-based healthcare service providers.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill results in a significant increase in State general fund expenditures, estimated at $25.6 million in FY 2025 and at least $35.5 million annually thereafter, to reimburse community-based service providers for their employer contributions. However, the one-year delay in program implementation leads to a temporary decrease in State expenditures (all funds) of $28.7 million in FY 2024 and $10.0 million in FY 2025 due to delayed employer contributions. FAMLI special fund revenues and expenditures are similarly shifted. Local government expenditures for employer contributions are also delayed by one year.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Department of Labor (MDL) is the primary agency responsible for the administration and implementation of the Family and Medical Leave Insurance (FAMLI) Program. The bill modifies MDL's administrative duties, requires the Secretary of Labor to conduct annual cost analyses, and sets timelines for contribution and benefit starts.

The bill explicitly requires the Maryland Department of Health (MDH) to reimburse certain community providers (licensed under Title 7 or 7.5) for the employer's share of FAMLI contributions. This creates a significant administrative and fiscal mandate for the department.

The Board of Public Works (comprising the Governor, Comptroller, and Treasurer) is tasked with determining whether to temporarily suspend annual increases in the maximum weekly benefit based on seasonally adjusted total employment and state revenue performance.

As the principal personnel agency for the State, DBM is impacted by the delay in state employer contributions for employees. The bill also has a significant fiscal impact on the General Fund, which DBM manages.

The Comptroller is required to report on the performance of State revenues to the Board of Public Works to help determine whether to suspend benefit increases. Additionally, the Comptroller sits on the Board of Public Works, which has a decision-making role under the bill.

The Treasurer's Office is involved in the issuance of benefit checks (though the bill modifies signature requirements) and the Treasurer serves on the Board of Public Works, which determines benefit adjustments.

The bill specifies that private employer plans may satisfy program requirements through insurance from an insurer authorized by the Maryland Insurance Commissioner, placing a regulatory or oversight connection to the MIA.
The OAG provides legal counsel to the Department of Labor and may be involved in enforcement actions or litigation regarding program compliance and benefit denials.
The Governor oversees the executive branch agencies (MDL, MDH, DBM) implementing the program and serves as a member of the Board of Public Works, which has specific duties under the bill.

Synopsis: Authorizing the Board of License Commissioners for Frederick County to issue a Class B-MGC (miniature golf course) beer, wine, and liquor license to a miniature golf course under certain circumstances; authorizing a license holder to sell beer, wine, and liquor for on-premises consumption under certain circumstances; requiring a license holder to submit an annual gross sales report for alcohol, golf games and food to the Board before a license may be renewed; and providing an annual license fee of $1,500.
Title: Frederick County – Alcoholic Beverages – Miniature Golf Course License

NarrowSubjects.Name: Fees -see also- Attys' Fees; Devt Fees & Taxes; Reimb Rates

bill_summary: This bill establishes a Class B–MGC (miniature golf course) beer, wine, and liquor license in Frederick County, allowing qualifying courses with at least 18 holes to sell alcoholic beverages for on-premises consumption. To maintain the license, businesses must ensure that alcoholic beverages do not exceed 35% of gross sales, while golf games and food must account for at least 50% and 15% of gross sales, respectively.
responsible_party: Frederick County Board of License Commissioners
stakeholders: Miniature golf course owners and operators in Frederick County, patrons of these courses, and the Frederick County Board of License Commissioners.
fiscal_impact_summary: Frederick County revenues are projected to increase by $1,500 annually starting in fiscal 2024, as one business is expected to apply for the new license. The annual license fee is set at $1,500. There is no fiscal impact on state finances, and the county can manage enforcement with existing resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the state's chief executive, the Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and signed this legislation (House Bill 989) into law as Chapter 420 of the 2023 Laws of Maryland.

The Comptroller of Maryland is explicitly tasked with regulating the alcohol, tobacco, and motor fuel industries in the state. This bill creates a new class of alcohol license (Class B-MGC) within the state's Alcoholic Beverages Article, falling under the Comptroller's broad regulatory and tax collection purview for the alcoholic beverages sector.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to state agencies, boards, and commissions. This includes the Board of License Commissioners for Frederick County, which is the primary body authorized by this state law to issue and regulate the new Class B-MGC licenses.

The Department of Commerce is responsible for stimulating the economy and supporting businesses. The fiscal note indicates that this bill may help miniature golf courses realize higher revenues through the sale of alcoholic beverages, impacting the economic viability of these small businesses in Frederick County.

Synopsis: Repealing the requirement in Frederick County that alcoholic beverages in a basket of cheer be produced in Maryland.
Title: Frederick County - Alcoholic Beverages - Basket of Cheer
bill_summary: This bill repeals the requirement that alcoholic beverages included in a 'basket of cheer' raffle prize in Frederick County must be produced in Maryland. It allows holders of certain per diem licenses to include any alcoholic beverages in these prize baskets, provided they are purchased from a licensed retailer.
responsible_party: Frederick County Board of License Commissioners
stakeholders: Holders of Class C per diem beer and wine licenses and Class C per diem beer, wine, and liquor licenses in Frederick County; organizations conducting benefit performances; and Frederick County alcoholic beverage retailers.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill has no impact on State finances and does not materially affect Frederick County operations or finances. The small business impact is considered minimal.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller of Maryland is the state's principal regulator of the alcohol industry and is responsible for enforcing state laws and regulations regarding alcoholic beverages and associated permits.

The bill repeals the requirement that alcoholic beverages in a 'basket of cheer' permit be produced in Maryland, which relates to the Department's mission of promoting local agricultural products and supporting the economic viability of Maryland agribusinesses.
The Governor's Office is responsible for the final review and signing of state legislation, including this bill which amends the Alcoholic Beverages Article of the Maryland Code.

Synopsis: Altering the quantity of certain alcoholic beverages an individual may consume under certain consumption permits issued in Frederick County.
Title: Frederick County - Alcoholic Beverages - Consumption Permits

NarrowSubjects.Name: Alcoholic Beverages -see also- AB-By Subd; Subst Abuse; etc.

bill_summary: This bill modifies the allowable consumption quantities for alcoholic beverages under Beer and Wine Consumption (BWC) and Beer, Wine, and Liquor Consumption (BWLC) permits in Frederick County. It permits a choice between a single standard serving or three smaller sample servings in various combinations.
responsible_party: Frederick County Board of License Commissioners
stakeholders: Class A license holders in Frederick County and individuals consuming alcoholic beverages on their premises.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill has no state fiscal impact. Local fiscal impact is not anticipated to be material to Frederick County's operations or finances. Permit fees for BWC and BWLC holders remain unchanged at $200 and $400 respectively.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller of Maryland is the principal state-level regulator of the alcohol industry. This bill modifies consumption permit regulations within the Alcoholic Beverages Article of the Maryland Code, which falls under the regulatory and enforcement scope of the Comptroller's office.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and is responsible for signing bills into law. The Governor approved and signed this legislation (Chapter 86).

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the Governor and the General Assembly on the constitutionality and legal sufficiency of legislation, including amendments to the state's Alcoholic Beverages Article.

Synopsis: Repealing certain provisions of law applicable to the State Department of Assessments and Taxation that prohibit the acceptance of articles of dissolution and issuance of a certificate of termination for certain corporations unless certain reports on personal property are filed with the Department; etc.
Title: Corporations - Filing Requirements for Dissolution and Termination of Registration or Qualification - Repeal

NarrowSubjects.Name: Corporations -see also- Municipal Corps; Public Corps & Inst

bill_summary: The bill repeals the requirement that corporations file personal property reports with the State Department of Assessments and Taxation (SDAT) as a prerequisite for the department to accept articles of dissolution or issue certificates of termination for foreign corporations.
responsible_party: State Department of Assessments and Taxation
stakeholders: Domestic and foreign corporations and the State Department of Assessments and Taxation
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, State general fund revenues are estimated to decrease by approximately $150,000 annually beginning in fiscal 2024. This decrease is attributed to an estimated 500 business entities per year no longer paying the $300 corporate filing fee for annual reports prior to dissolving or terminating their registration. No impact on State expenditures or local government finances is expected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the state's chief financial officer, the Comptroller is responsible for the oversight of state revenues. This bill has a direct fiscal impact, reducing general fund revenues by approximately $150,000 annually due to the loss of corporate filing fees.

DBM is the principal fiscal agency responsible for revenue estimation and long-term fiscal planning. The bill's $150,000 annual reduction in general fund revenue must be accounted for in the state's budget and revenue projections.

The Department of Commerce is Maryland's primary economic development agency. Changes to the filing requirements for the dissolution and termination of corporations impact the state's business regulatory environment and ease of doing business.

The OAG serves as the primary legal representative for the state and provides legal counsel to all state agencies, including the State Department of Assessments and Taxation (SDAT), which is the primary body implementing this bill's changes to corporate law.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch, including the primary implementing agency (SDAT), and the Governor signed the bill into law as part of his executive duties.

The Maryland Tax Court provides administrative review for disputes involving final decisions of taxing authorities. While the bill repeals a filing barrier, it relates to personal property tax reports which are within the Court's adjudicative scope for related appeals.

The OLA conducts fiscal compliance audits of state agencies; it will need to account for the change in filing requirements and the associated reduction in revenue collection during future audits of the State Department of Assessments and Taxation.

Synopsis: Altering certain provisions related to the rates the Department of State Police sets for tow companies involved in certain police-initiated towing; establishing the Committee on Rate Setting and Complaint Resolution for Police-Initiated Medium-Duty and Heavy-Duty Towing and Recovery; and requiring the Committee, on or before December 1, 2023, to recommend approved rates to the Department of State Police that should be charged for police-initiated towing and recovery services.
Title: Commercial Vehicles - Police-Initiated Towing - Alterations

NarrowSubjects.Name: Committees and Commissions -see also- Political Committees
Motor Vehicles -see also- Aband Veh; Ambulances; Buses; etc.

bill_summary: This bill regulates police-initiated towing and recovery for medium-duty and heavy-duty commercial vehicles. It establishes the Committee on Rate Setting and Complaint Resolution within the Department of State Police to recommend maximum towing rates and complaint resolution processes. The bill bans 'per pound billing' for these services, requires the Department of State Police to establish approved rates by January 1, 2024, and outlines procedures for the release of vehicles and cargo during fee disputes.
stakeholders: Commercial vehicle owners and operators, authorized medium-duty and heavy-duty tow companies, and the Maryland Department of State Police.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, State general fund expenditures increase by $44,700 in FY 2024 to hire a part-time administrator to support the newly established Committee on Rate Setting and Complaint Resolution and handle related administrative tasks. Costs are projected to increase annually due to inflation and salary adjustments, reaching $58,000 by FY 2028. Local government operations and finances are not expected to be materially affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill primarily impacts the Department of State Police (DSP), which is responsible for establishing the approved rates for police-initiated towing, maintaining the authorized tow list, adjudicating complaints against tow companies, and providing staff support for the newly established Committee.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly establishes the Committee on Rate Setting and Complaint Resolution for Police-Initiated Medium-Duty and Heavy-Duty Towing and Recovery, which falls under this category of advisory bodies.

The Secretary of Transportation is responsible for appointing a representative from the MDTA Police to the new committee, and the department oversees the State Highway Administration, which also has a seat on the committee.
The SHA Administrator is tasked with appointing a representative to the new committee, and the agency is directly involved in highway maintenance and clearing disabled commercial vehicles.
The MDTA is explicitly represented on the committee through its police force, and the agency manages toll facilities where police-initiated towing frequently occurs.

The Insurance Commissioner is responsible for appointing a representative to the committee, which will recommend rates and complaint resolution processes that impact insurance claims and coverage for towing services.

The bill requires DSP to develop a process to adjudicate complaints and suspend or remove tow companies from the list; such contested administrative actions typically involve the Office of Administrative Hearings for impartial review.

The OAG serves as the legal counsel for the Department of State Police, the Department of Transportation, and the Maryland Insurance Administration, and would likely be involved in drafting regulations and reviewing the legal framework for the new rates and complaint processes.

The fiscal note indicates a need for general fund expenditures to support a part-time administrator position at the Department of State Police to staff the committee and manage the new requirements, which falls under DBM's personnel and fiscal oversight.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive agencies responsible for implementing the bill, including the Maryland State Police and the Department of Transportation.
The bill mentions requirements for cargo clean-up and the release of cargo, which may involve MDE oversight if the cargo includes hazardous materials or impacts environmental resources.

Synopsis: Authorizing the governing body of Wicomico County to create a sanitary district.
Title: Wicomico County - Sanitary District - Authorization

NarrowSubjects.Name: Sanitary Districts -see also- Wash Sub Sanitary District

bill_summary: This bill authorizes the governing body of Wicomico County to establish sanitary districts within the county to manage and provide water and sewer services, primarily to address public health concerns related to failing septic systems.
stakeholders: Residents and property owners in Wicomico County, particularly those using septic systems, and the Wicomico County government.
fiscal_impact_summary: State effect is none. Locally, the bill may lead to a significant increase in Wicomico County expenditures and revenues if sanitary districts are established. While the county anticipates a significant financial impact to resolve water and sewerage issues, specific dollar estimates for the total implementation cost are currently indeterminate and unavailable.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly amends the Environment Article, which MDE administers. The agency is responsible for overseeing public water and sewer systems and providing technical and financial assistance for environmental infrastructure improvements.

The authorization of sanitary districts aims to address failing septic systems that pose public health risks from groundwater contamination, which aligns with the department's mission to protect public health and oversee local health departments.

MES provides technical and operational support to local governments for water and wastewater treatment; it may serve as a partner or provider for the infrastructure projects managed by the new sanitary districts.

The agency promotes sustainable growth and provides technical assistance to local governments on land use and infrastructure planning, which are critical to the formation and management of sanitary districts.
Wicomico is a rural county, and the council focuses on addressing unique rural challenges, including infrastructure development and healthcare access in these jurisdictions.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Council on the Chesapeake Bay
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The council coordinates interagency efforts for bay restoration; sanitary districts play a key role in reducing nutrient runoff that impacts the Chesapeake and coastal bays.
This multi-agency initiative coordinates sustainable development efforts across MDE and MDP, guiding local decision-making regarding land use and resource conservation related to infrastructure.
The OAG provides legal counsel to the General Assembly and executive agencies regarding the implementation of environmental and public health laws.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and is responsible for the final review and signing of the legislation.

Synopsis: Reducing from 150 yards to 50 yards the size of the safety zone for archery hunters in Howard County who are under the authority of a deer management permit or who are actively participating in a hunting program administered by the county within which archery hunting may not take place except under certain circumstances; and requiring certain archery hunters in Howard County to be in an elevated position when hunting any wild bird or mammal within 50 to 150 yards of certain buildings.
Title: Howard County – Archery Hunting – Safety Zone and Position of Archery Hunter Ho. Co. 15–23

NarrowSubjects.Name: Housing -see also- Apartments; Condos; Mobile & Manuf  Homes

bill_summary: This bill reduces the archery hunting safety zone in Howard County from 150 yards to 50 yards for hunters acting under a deer management permit or participating in a county-administered hunting program. It also mandates that these hunters use an elevated position to ensure a downward trajectory when hunting within 50 to 150 yards of dwellings, churches, schools, or other occupied buildings.
stakeholders: Archery hunters in Howard County with deer management permits or in county-administered programs, and property owners or occupants of buildings near hunting areas.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is not expected to materially affect Maryland State or local operations or finances. No specific revenue or expenditure estimates were provided in the Fiscal Note because the financial impact is considered negligible.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This bill amends the Natural Resources Article of the Maryland Code. The Department of Natural Resources (DNR), specifically through its Wildlife and Heritage Service, issues the deer management permits referenced in the bill and manages hunting regulations and safety zones statewide. Furthermore, DNR's Natural Resources Police are responsible for enforcing the hunting safety and elevated position requirements established by this legislation.

The bill's focus on deer management permits is directly relevant to the agricultural community, as these permits are primary tools used by farmers and landowners to mitigate crop damage and maintain the economic viability of agribusiness, which the Department of Agriculture supports.
The Governor's Office oversees the Department of Natural Resources and the executive branch's implementation of state laws. The Governor also reviewed and signed this legislation into law.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the Department of Natural Resources and the General Assembly regarding the implementation and enforcement of statutory changes to hunting laws.

Synopsis: Providing that, notwithstanding any other provision of law, except for regulations issued by the Department of the Environment, no provision of the State building code or other law or regulation may prohibit or otherwise limit the use of a refrigerant if the refrigerant is designated as acceptable for use under federal listing requirements and any appliance containing the refrigerant meets federal safety standards and use conditions.
Title: Public Safety – Refrigerants – Limitations on Use

NarrowSubjects.Name: Hazardous and Toxic Substances -see also- Asbestos; Radiatn

bill_summary: This bill prohibits state building codes and other regulations from limiting the use of refrigerants that are federally approved and used in appliances meeting federal safety standards, though the Maryland Department of the Environment may still issue its own regulations regarding these substances.
stakeholders: Appliance manufacturers, HVAC technicians, and owners of commercial and residential properties.
fiscal_impact_summary: The Maryland Department of Legislative Services reports that the bill will not materially affect state or local finances. The Maryland Department of the Environment indicates that it can manage implementation using its existing budgeted resources. Small business impact is expected to be minimal.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly names the Department of the Environment as the sole agency with the authority to issue regulations that may prohibit or limit refrigerants otherwise allowed by this legislation. The agency is also the primary body responsible for regulating greenhouse gas emissions and environmental protection in Maryland.

The Department of Labor is responsible for incorporating the Maryland Building Performance Standards (MBPS) and the International Mechanical Code (IMC). The bill directly impacts these standards by prohibiting them from restricting certain federally approved refrigerants.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to state agencies, including the Department of Labor and the Department of the Environment, regarding the interpretation of these new statutory limitations and their alignment with federal laws such as the Clean Air Act.

As the agency responsible for the maintenance and construction of state-owned facilities, the Department of General Services is impacted by changes to the types of refrigerants that can be used in the HVAC and refrigeration systems of those buildings.

The agency oversees housing development and community revitalization programs; changes to building standards and mechanical code requirements for refrigerants affect the design and construction of housing projects it supports.

Synopsis: Authorizing Prince George's County to exercise powers of eminent domain to acquire and develop or redevelop, for a public purpose, certain neglected property located in the county that has been designated as a transit-oriented development and is located within a business improvement district; and prohibiting land or property taken by the county through the use of eminent domain under the provisions of the Act to be taken without just compensation, as agreed on between the parties, or awarded by a jury.
Title: Prince George's County - Land Use - Development of Neglected Property PG 406-23

NarrowSubjects.Name: Commerce and Business -see also- Dealers; Elec. Comm.; etc.

bill_summary: This bill authorizes Prince George's County to exercise the power of eminent domain to acquire and develop 'neglected property' located within areas designated as transit-oriented development and within business improvement districts. Neglected property is defined as real property that is abandoned, blighted, or condemned and zoned for commercial, industrial, residential, or nonresidential use. The acquisition must be for a public purpose, including private development consistent with a public purpose, and requires the payment of just compensation to the property owner.
stakeholders: Owners of abandoned, blighted, or condemned properties in Prince George's County; residents and businesses in transit-oriented development areas and business improvement districts.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, the bill does not directly affect State or local government finances. While the county is required to pay just compensation for property taken through eminent domain, the fiscal note identifies no specific revenue or expenditure estimates.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill centers on property designated as 'transit-oriented development' (TOD). Under Maryland law, TODs are specifically designated by the Secretary of Transportation. Furthermore, the bill explicitly includes light rail stops on the Purple Line, which is a major project managed by MDOT.

The bill amends the Land Use Article and concerns the development of neglected properties and transit-oriented development, which fall under the department's mission to promote sustainable growth, land use planning, and technical assistance to local governments.

The department is responsible for community revitalization and urban infrastructure. The bill's focus on acquiring and redeveloping neglected, blighted, or abandoned property for economic development aligns with DHCD's core mission.

The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies regarding the application of state laws, including land use and eminent domain. The agency was consulted in the preparation of the fiscal note for this bill.

Eminent domain proceedings often involve the judicial system to determine just compensation when agreements cannot be reached. The fiscal note identifies the Judiciary as an affected entity for information purposes.

The bill's purpose is to facilitate economic development within business improvement districts. As the state's primary economic development agency, Commerce has a relevant interest in the redevelopment of blighted areas into commercial or industrial assets.

Synopsis: Requiring educational professionals employed by a county board of education, the Baltimore City Board of School Commissioners, or a county public library system who transfer to the Juvenile Services Education Program to be given credit as State employees for certain years of service for the purpose of establishing leave accrual rates; authorizing an individual who transfers to the Program to transfer leave balances in excess of a certain limit under certain circumstances; and applying the Act retroactively.
Title: Juvenile Services Education Program - Transfer of Locally Employed Educational Professionals

NarrowSubjects.Name: Committees and Commissions -see also- Political Committees
Education -see also- Driver Ed; Higher Ed; Special Ed; etc
Salaries and Compensation -see also- Overtime; Reimb. Rates

bill_summary: This bill allows educational professionals, such as teachers and librarians employed by local school boards or libraries, to transfer to the State's Juvenile Services Education Program (JSEP) without losing their accumulated leave or seniority. It requires the State to credit their years of local service when calculating leave accrual, maintain their hourly pay rate, and place them in comparable positions. These provisions apply retroactively to individuals who transferred on or after July 1, 2022.
stakeholders: Educational professionals employed by county boards of education, the Baltimore City Board of School Commissioners, or county public library systems who transfer to the Juvenile Services Education Program.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is not expected to have a material effect on State operations or finances, and it has no direct effect on local operations or finances. The Department of Juvenile Services (DJS) indicates that any administrative costs associated with tracking unique leave rules can be absorbed within existing resources. While the bill applies retroactively to July 1, 2022, state agencies are currently unaware of any employees who would be impacted by the retroactive provision.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Juvenile Services Education Program (JSEP) is housed within the Department of Juvenile Services. The bill directly impacts DJS operations by mandating how the agency must handle the transfer, compensation, and position classification of educational professionals joining the program from local jurisdictions.

As the state's central personnel agency, DBM is responsible for managing State employee benefits and positions. The bill requires the creation of specific Position Identification Numbers (PINs) and requires DBM to track and apply special leave accrual rules based on prior local service, which the fiscal note identifies as an administrative responsibility for the department.

The bill applies to educational professionals whose standards are established by the State Board of Education. Furthermore, the Juvenile Services Education Program was recently transferred from MSDE to DJS, and this legislation addresses personnel matters stemming from that transition.

The bill specifically includes librarians and public library associates from county library systems who transfer to the Juvenile Services Education Program. As the agency providing leadership and coordination for the state's 24 public library systems, the Maryland State Library Agency is relevant to the personnel standards and transition of these employees.

Synopsis: Requiring the Maryland Transit Administration to submit a report by December 1, 2023, and each year thereafter on assaults on public transit operators to each local executive authority, the State's Attorney for each county, and certain committees of the General Assembly; and requiring the report to include information on the nature of each assault, the mode of transit involved, the location of the assault, whether the police were involved, and the outcome of any investigation.
Title: Transportation – Assaults on Public Transit Operators – Report

NarrowSubjects.Name: Transportation -see also- Aircraft; Airports; Boats; etc
Violence -see also- Domestic Violence; Harassment; Threats
Work, Labor, and Employment -see also- Col Bar; Holiday; etc

bill_summary: This bill requires the Maryland Transit Administration (MTA) to submit an annual report on assaults against public transit operators, including those employed by the MTA, the Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Authority (WMATA), and local political subdivisions. The report must include details on the nature and location of assaults, police involvement, investigation outcomes, comparisons with other states, and a review of industry best practices for preventing such incidents.
stakeholders: Public transit operators, transit station managers, local executive authorities, State's Attorneys, and the Maryland General Assembly
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, State Transportation Trust Fund (TTF) expenditures will increase by $50,000 in FY 2024 only. This cost is for the MTA to hire a consultant to evaluate the feasibility of establishing a statewide local transit safety officer for the initial report. Subsequent reporting requirements are expected to be handled using existing resources. There is no impact on State revenues or local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly mandates the Maryland Transit Administration to compile and submit the annual report on assaults on public transit operators and to conduct a feasibility study for a statewide local transit safety officer.

As the parent agency of the Maryland Transit Administration, the Department of Transportation oversees the Transportation Trust Fund, which the fiscal note identifies as being impacted by a $50,000 expenditure for the feasibility study.

The Department of Budget and Management is responsible for state budget oversight and will be involved in the execution and monitoring of the fiscal expenditures related to the new transit safety study.

The reporting requirements include data on whether police were involved in responding to transit assaults and the outcome of investigations, areas where the State Police provides primary or allied law enforcement support.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This office coordinates state public safety and criminal justice strategies; data on assaults against transit operators is relevant to their policy development and efforts to reduce crime and improve safety.

The Department of Labor oversees workplace safety and labor laws (MOSH); physical assaults on public transit employees are a significant occupational safety issue that falls within their regulatory interests.

As the administrator for workers' compensation claims for State of Maryland employees, the Injured Workers' Insurance Fund is directly impacted by data and mitigation strategies related to workplace injuries caused by assaults on transit operators.

Synopsis: Authorizing an applicant to appeal a certain decision issued by the State Public Information Compliance Board; authorizing a party aggrieved by a final judgment of a circuit court in a proceeding for judicial review of a certain decision of the Board to appeal to the Appellate Court of Maryland.
Title: Public Information Act - Decisions of the State Public Information Act Compliance Board - Appeals

NarrowSubjects.Name: Committees and Commissions -see also- Political Committees

bill_summary: This bill authorizes an applicant who requests a public record to appeal a decision made by the State Public Information Act Compliance Board to a circuit court. It also allows any party aggrieved by a circuit court's final judgment in such a proceeding to further appeal to the Appellate Court of Maryland and clarifies the venue for appeals related to complaints of frivolous or bad-faith requests.
responsible_party: State Public Information Act Compliance Board
stakeholders: Individuals and governmental units requesting public records, custodians of government records, and the Maryland judicial system.
fiscal_impact_summary: The Fiscal Note indicates that the bill is not anticipated to materially affect State or local government operations or finances. No specific dollar estimates were provided as the impact is expected to be negligible.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly modifies judicial procedures by establishing that an applicant can appeal a decision of the State Public Information Act Compliance Board to a circuit court and subsequently to the Appellate Court of Maryland, affecting court dockets and jurisdictional processes.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This agency category encompasses the State Public Information Act Compliance Board (PIACB), whose decisions, authority, and the legal pathways for appealing its rulings are the primary focus of the bill.

The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies and boards, including the PIACB. It also publishes the Public Information Act Manual and represents state agencies (custodians) in judicial review proceedings.
The Governor appoints the members of the State Public Information Act Compliance Board and oversees the executive departments that serve as custodians of public records subject to this legislation.

The bill stipulates that if a court finds a custodian acted arbitrarily or capriciously in withholding a record, a finding is sent to the appointing authority for disciplinary action; DBM oversees state personnel policies and disciplinary frameworks.
This office assists the Governor in recruiting and vetting members for the various boards and commissions, including the State Public Information Act Compliance Board.

Synopsis: Establishing in Harford County a performing arts theater beer and wine license that authorizes the holder to sell or serve beer and wine in certain performing arts theaters at retail for on-premises consumption; and establishing an annual license fee of $500.
Title: Harford County - Alcoholic Beverages - Performing Arts Theater License

NarrowSubjects.Name: Fees -see also- Attys' Fees; Devt Fees & Taxes; Reimb Rates
Food -see also- Meat, Poultry, Seafood; Milk

bill_summary: This bill establishes a performing arts theater beer and wine license in Harford County, specifically for theaters operated by nonprofit organizations. The license allows for the retail sale and on-premises consumption of beer and wine during, and for one hour before and after, a performance, provided snacks are also offered for sale.
responsible_party: Harford County Board of License Commissioners
stakeholders: Nonprofit performing arts theaters in Harford County and their patrons
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, there is no State effect. Harford County revenues are estimated to increase by $500 annually beginning in fiscal 2024, based on the anticipated issuance of one performing arts theater license. Any additional enforcement activities can be managed with the county's existing resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the state's principal tax collector and regulator of the alcohol industry, the Comptroller is responsible for oversight and tax compliance related to the newly established beer and wine license category.

The OAG serves as the primary legal representative for the state and provides legal counsel to boards and commissions on the interpretation and enforcement of alcoholic beverage laws in the Maryland Code.
This department oversees the state's arts and cultural institutions; the bill impacts the operational capabilities of nonprofit performing arts theaters, which are key constituents.
The Maryland Office of Tourism Development promotes cultural attractions; providing alcoholic beverage options can enhance the appeal and economic viability of these tourism destinations.

The Governor's Office is responsible for overseeing the executive branch and appointing the members of the Harford County Board of License Commissioners, which is the entity empowered to issue this new license.
The Office of Appointments assists the Governor in recruiting and vetting the individuals who serve on the Harford County Board of License Commissioners.

The Secretary of State oversees the registration and regulation of charitable organizations; since the performing arts theater license is limited to nonprofit organizations, they fall under the general oversight of this office.

Synopsis: Altering the quota used to determine the maximum number of certain alcoholic beverages licenses that the Board of License Commissioners for Harford County may issue from one for every 3,000 individuals to one for every 4,000 individuals.
Title: Harford County - Alcoholic Beverages - Alteration of License Quota
bill_summary: This bill alters the population quota for alcoholic beverages licenses in Harford County by increasing the required population from 3,000 to 4,000 individuals per license. It also limits the Board of License Commissioners to issuing only one of any Class A, A-1, or A-2 license per population unit, rather than allowing one of each per unit.
responsible_party: Board of License Commissioners for Harford County
stakeholders: Alcoholic beverages license applicants and holders in Harford County, and the Harford County Board of License Commissioners.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, the bill has no state fiscal impact and is not expected to materially affect Harford County finances or operations.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly requires that the population figures used by the Harford County Board of License Commissioners to determine alcoholic beverage license quotas be those specified by the Maryland Department of Health.

The Comptroller is the state's principal regulator of the alcohol industry. Although the bill concerns a local county board's license quota, the Comptroller's office has broad oversight of alcohol licensing, revenue collection, and industry regulation in Maryland.

Synopsis: Establishing a 6-day and a 7-day Class HC (health club) beer and wine license in Harford County; authorizing the Board of License Commissioners for Harford County to issue the license to a person who sells health club services; exempting the holder of the license from certain distance requirements related to places of worship and schools; establishing an annual fee of $1,300 for a 6-day license and $1,400 for a 7-day license; etc.
Title: Harford County - Alcoholic Beverages - Class HC (Health Club) License
bill_summary: This bill establishes 6-day and 7-day Class HC (health club) beer and wine licenses in Harford County. Eligible facilities must offer health club services, have at least 150 dues-paying members, and provide amenities such as a swimming pool or pickleball courts. The license allows for the sale and on-premises consumption of beer and wine between 1 p.m. and 9 p.m. and exempts these establishments from certain distance requirements from schools and places of worship.
responsible_party: Harford County Board of License Commissioners
stakeholders: Health club facilities in Harford County and their members/patrons
fiscal_impact_summary: Harford County revenues are estimated to increase by $1,400 annually beginning in fiscal 2024, based on the expectation that one business will obtain a 7-day Class HC license. The annual fee for a 6-day license is $1,300, and the fee for a 7-day license is $1,400. The bill has no state fiscal impact, and local monitoring can be handled with existing resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the state's principal tax collector and regulator of the alcohol industry, the Comptroller's Office is responsible for overseeing the regulatory framework under which local alcoholic beverage licenses operate, including the collection of relevant taxes and the regulation of wholesalers from whom the license holder must purchase products.

The Harford County Board of License Commissioners, which is the entity authorized by this bill to issue the Class HC licenses, is a body appointed by the Governor. The Office of Appointments is responsible for the recruitment and vetting of candidates for this board.

The OAG provides legal counsel for state laws and oversees consumer protection. This bill specifically references 'health club services' as defined in the Commercial Law Article, which is regulated by the OAG's Consumer Protection Division through its Health Club Services unit.

The Governor serves as the final authority for signing the bill into law and possesses the constitutional authority to appoint members to the Harford County Board of License Commissioners, which implements the bill's provisions locally.

Synopsis: Establishing the Commission on Hate Crime Response and Prevention to develop strategies to prevent and respond to hate crime activity and evaluate State laws and policies relating to hate crimes; and requiring the Commission to report to the General Assembly on or before December 1 each year, beginning in 2024, on legislative recommendations to address hate crimes in the State.
Title: Hate Crimes - Commission on Hate Crime Response and Prevention - Establishment

NarrowSubjects.Name: Committees and Commissions -see also- Political Committees
Crimes and Punishments -see also- Penalties and Sentnc; etc.
Laws and Ordinances -see also- Pub Local Laws; Uniform Laws

bill_summary: This bill establishes the Commission on Hate Crime Response and Prevention within the Office of the Attorney General. The commission is tasked with developing strategies to prevent and respond to hate crimes, evaluating relevant state laws and policies, and submitting annual policy and legislative recommendations to the State Department of Education and the General Assembly.
responsible_party: Maryland Office of the Attorney General
stakeholders: Maryland residents, community organizations representing diverse ethnic and religious groups, law enforcement agencies, and the State Department of Education.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $136,300 in fiscal 2025 to employ a permanent assistant Attorney General to staff the commission. This follows a fiscal 2024 increase of $114,400 in federal fund expenditures for a contractual position. The bill establishes a mandated appropriation starting in fiscal 2025. Local government finances are not expected to be materially affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill requires the Governor to include specific funding in the annual state budget starting in FY 2025 to implement the Commission, hire an Assistant Attorney General, and operate the office.

The Commission on Hate Crime Response and Prevention is established within the Office of the Attorney General. The Attorney General appoints the members, chairs the commission, and the office provides staffing and operational support.
As the principal fiscal and personnel agency, DBM is responsible for the budget execution of the mandated appropriation and the creation of the new personnel position required by the bill.
The Commission is mandated to submit an annual report to the State Department of Education containing policy recommendations to address hate crimes occurring in schools.
The Maryland Commission on Civil Rights is explicitly named as a required member of the Commission on Hate Crime Response and Prevention.

The Maryland Center for School Safety is explicitly named as a required member of the Commission and the Commission's work involves reporting specific recommendations regarding school-based hate crimes.

The bill includes a representative from the Maryland Coordination and Analysis Center (MCAC) as a member; MCAC is the state fusion center operated by the Maryland State Police. The Commission's mission to evaluate hate crime laws and response also aligns with MSP's public safety functions.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes a new permanent commission (Commission on Hate Crime Response and Prevention) which falls under this collective designation for state advisory and policy bodies.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: GOCPP is the primary coordinating body for public safety and criminal justice strategies. The Commission's task to develop strategies to prevent and respond to hate crime activity directly overlaps with GOCPP's mission.

Synopsis: Altering the maximum fines for smoking cannabis in a public place; prohibiting a law enforcement officer from initiating a stop or a search of a person, a motor vehicle, or a vessel based solely on certain factors; prohibiting, under certain circumstances, a law enforcement officer from conducting a search of a certain area of a motor vehicle or vessel; providing that evidence obtained in violation of certain provisions of the Act is not admissible in certain proceedings; etc.
Title: Criminal Law and Procedure - Cannabis - Fines for Smoking in Public, Stops, and Searches
Status: Enacted under Article II, Section 17(c) of the Maryland Constitution - Chapter 802

NarrowSubjects.Name: Investigations and Inquiries -see also- Crim Bckgrnd Invest

bill_summary: This bill prohibits law enforcement officers from stopping or searching individuals, vehicles, or vessels based solely on the odor of cannabis, possession of a personal use amount, or the proximity of cash to cannabis. It also reduces the maximum civil fines for smoking cannabis in public from $250 to $50 for a first offense and from $500 to $150 for subsequent offenses. Furthermore, it stipulates that evidence obtained in violation of these provisions is inadmissible in court proceedings.
responsible_party: Maryland law enforcement agencies, the Judiciary, and the Office of the Public Defender
stakeholders: Individuals possessing or using cannabis, law enforcement officers, and the Maryland court system
fiscal_impact_summary: State and local revenues and expenditures are expected to decrease minimally. Revenue decreases are attributed to lower fines for smoking cannabis in public and a potential reduction in overall fines collected due to fewer arrests. Expenditure decreases are expected from reduced law enforcement and judicial workloads, as well as lower incarceration costs. While the Fiscal Note identifies a monthly cost of $4,970 per inmate, specific aggregate dollar estimates for the bill's total impact are unavailable.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill significantly impacts the judiciary by altering the maximum fines for smoking cannabis in public, establishing new rules for the admissibility of evidence in court (the exclusionary rule), and requiring the courts to process cases based on revised reasonable suspicion and probable cause standards.

As the primary state law enforcement agency, the Maryland State Police are directly affected by the new restrictions on initiating stops or searches based on the odor of cannabis, possession limits, or the proximity of cash. This bill fundamentally changes their search and seizure procedures.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Office of the Public Defender is directly impacted because the bill's changes to the exclusionary rule and the legality of searches will be central to the legal defense of indigent clients in cannabis-related cases.

MDOT is highly relevant as it oversees several law enforcement components—the MTA Police and the MDTA Police—which are subject to the bill's search and stop restrictions. Additionally, its Motor Vehicle Administration (MVA) handles point assessments for impaired driving violations mentioned in the fiscal note.

The bill specifically mentions 'vessels' in its restrictions on stops and searches. The Natural Resources Police, who patrol Maryland's waterways, will have to adjust their enforcement protocols for impaired operation and cannabis possession on boats.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services

bill_summary: This bill revises the governance of the Prince George's County Board of Education. Key changes include expanding the voting rights of the student board member to include school budgets and boundaries, and altering the student member's election process to include a general vote by students in grades 6 through 12. The bill also increases compensation for board members beginning in 2026, establishes a two-term limit for elected members, and requires the board to provide and pay for legal counsel for members sued for actions taken in their official capacity. Additionally, it mandates professional development for board members and requires the school system to set and evaluate annual performance goals.

stakeholders: Students in grades 6 through 12, Board of Education members and candidates, and Prince George's County Public Schools personnel.
fiscal_impact_summary: State finances are not affected. Additionally, MSDE oversees the leadership and policy implementation for all 24 local school systems, including the governance and disciplinary voting changes mandated for Prince George's County.

The bill significantly alters the Governor's executive authority by removing the requirement that the Governor approve the removal of a member of the Prince George’s County Board of Education by the State Board of Education. This impacts the Governor's role in overseeing local board integrity and administrative appointments.

The OAG serves as the chief legal counsel to the State Board of Education and the Department of Education. This bill's changes to the board member removal process and the explicit provisions for judicial review in the Circuit Court for Prince George’s County directly involve the OAG's role in providing legal advice and representing state educational bodies in litigation.

bill_summary: This bill increases the severance tax on oysters harvested from Maryland's natural oyster bars (excluding the Potomac River) from $1 to $2 per bushel. It also raises the inspection tax on marketable oysters shipped out of state from 30 cents to $1 per bushel. The legislation mandates that $1 of every $2 collected from the severance tax be used by county oyster committees in specific counties for the repletion of natural oyster bars and repeals an obsolete 1982 tax provision.
stakeholders: Commercial oyster harvesters, buyers, shippers, and county oyster committees in Anne Arundel, Baltimore, Calvert, Charles, Dorchester, Kent, Queen Anne’s, Somerset, St. Mary’s, Talbot, and Wicomico counties.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the fiscal note, State special fund revenues and expenditures are projected to increase by approximately $580,900 annually starting in fiscal 2024. This increase is driven by higher tax collections that will be dedicated to the repletion of natural oyster bars. There is no impact on local government finances as county oyster committees are not considered local government entities.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DNR is the primary agency responsible for managing Maryland's fisheries and the Fisheries Research and Development Fund. The bill tasks the Department with collecting the increased severance and inspection taxes and overseeing the repletion of natural oyster bars.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly mandates that $1 of every $2 collected from the severance tax be used by the County Oyster Committees in specified counties for the repletion of natural oyster bars.

The bill has a notable fiscal impact, increasing special fund revenues and expenditures by approximately $580,900 annually. DBM is responsible for supervising budget execution and long-term fiscal planning related to these funds.

As the state's principal tax collector and chief financial officer, the Comptroller oversees the collection of state revenues, including those directed to special funds like the Fisheries Research and Development Fund.

The agency supports the economic viability of resource-based industries, including the seafood industry. The increased taxes and repletion efforts directly affect the economic conditions of Maryland's commercial oystermen.

The MDE is responsible for environmental restoration and water quality. Oyster repletion is a critical component of environmental efforts to restore the health of the Chesapeake Bay and its tributaries.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Agricultural & Resource-Based Industry Development Corp.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Council on the Chesapeake Bay
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Council advises the Governor on the management and restoration of the Chesapeake Bay. Oyster repletion and management are central topics for the Council's interagency restoration strategies.

Synopsis: Authorizing the Department of Natural Resources to allow a person to hunt game birds and mammals on each Sunday of the game bird and game mammal seasons from 30 minutes before sunrise until 10:30 a.m. in Wicomico County; authorizing the Department to allow Sunday hunting in Wicomico County on public land, subject to certain time restrictions; and adding Wicomico County to the list of counties in which the safety zone for archery hunters extends 50 yards from certain structures occupied by human beings.

bill_summary: This bill authorizes the Department of Natural Resources to allow Sunday hunting of game birds and mammals on private and designated public lands in Wicomico County, primarily from 30 minutes before sunrise until 10:30 a.m., with specific exceptions for deer firearms and bow seasons. Additionally, it reduces the archery hunting safety zone in Wicomico County from 150 yards to 50 yards from dwellings, churches, and other occupied buildings.
stakeholders: Hunters, property owners, and small businesses in Wicomico County
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, the bill is not expected to materially affect State or local operations or finances. Small business impacts are expected to be minimal overall, though potentially meaningful for certain businesses in Wicomico County due to increased hunting-related expenditures and reduced deer-related damage to crops and vehicles.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DNR is the primary implementing agency for this bill. It is explicitly authorized to allow Sunday hunting in Wicomico County, designate public lands for this purpose, and manage the associated time restrictions and safety regulations.
The OAG provides legal counsel to the Department of Natural Resources and would be responsible for reviewing the legality and enforcement of updated hunting regulations and safety zone modifications.

Expanding hunting opportunities, particularly for deer, directly benefits the agricultural community by reducing crop damage, which aligns with the department's mission to support the economic viability of farming.

The fiscal note highlights that hunters contribute significantly to local economies through trip-related expenditures. Authorizing more hunting days in Wicomico County can enhance tourism-related revenue for the region.

The RMC is dedicated to addressing the challenges of rural counties like Wicomico. The bill's potential to reduce agricultural damage and boost rural economic activity through hunting falls within their advocacy and stewardship interests.
The judicial branch may handle cases involving violations of the updated Sunday hunting laws or the newly defined 50-yard archery hunting safety zones.
The reduction in the deer population facilitated by expanded hunting can lead to a decrease in deer-vehicle collisions on state-maintained highways, improving overall traffic safety.
